_honestyNote:
WHAT THIS FILM CLAIMS, AND WHAT HAD TO CHANGE BEFORE IT COULD.

1. THE VOICE. The previous cut opened on 'An AI with a face, a voice and a body.'
   Two of those were on screen. The third was not true of a default install:
   ttsConfig.ts defaulted `mode` to 'pocket' against http://localhost:8000,
   nothing in this repo starts a Pocket TTS server, and generatePocketAudio's
   network-failure path marked every message `status: 'error'` and dropped it.
   Its own console warning said so — 'speech is disabled … or set
   VITE_TTS_MODE=browser'. A clean checkout was mute.

   Settled by fixing the PRODUCT, not by deleting the word: ttsService now
   degrades to speechSynthesis when the configured backend is unreachable and
   the browser can speak. `browser` mode was already fully implemented; it just
   had to be reachable without editing an env var. Covered by two tests in
   ttsService.dom.test.ts.

   The film still does not SAY 'a voice' over a frame, because a silent product
   screen cannot show one. The claim now sits in the recap, next to the thing
   that makes it true, and the title card claims only what the picture carries.

2. THE COUNTS. Verified in animationClips.ts: 6 VRMA + 34 GLB + 7 feminine = 47
   clips, and 5 providers in SettingsPanel PROVIDERS (proxy, ollama, openai,
   mlc, script). But NO SINGLE AVATAR LOADS ALL 47 — a VRM gets VRMA_CLIPS (6),
   a GLB rig gets GLB_CLIPS (34), a feminine rig gets GLB_ALL_CLIPS. So the
   recap chip says 'Clip library', and the narration says 'library'. It must
   never be phrased as what this avatar can do.

   EnvironmentPreset is 'none' | 'datacenter-1970s' — that is one optional room
   plus the plain studio, not 'two environments'. Filmed and worded as one room.

3. THE A-POSE. The committed frames showed the avatar in bind pose with splayed
   hands, and it was NOT a capture-timing artefact. capture.config.mjs hazard 12
   measured it: under SwiftShader the mixer never drives the rig at any settle
   (bind pose identical at 1s through 24s), while on ANGLE/Metal the avatar
   greets and settles into its idle. It was the renderer. The launch shim now
   appends the ANGLE flags and refuses the capture if it still landed on
   software, so these plates are shot on hardware GL.

4. PROP_NEEDS_REEXPORT is untouched. It excludes the two diorama props whose
   GLBs do not contain the machines their filenames claim; removing anything
   from it would put a mislabelled object in frame.

5. THESE SHOTS ARE NOT BYTE-STABLE, and this cut does not pretend otherwise —
   see hazard 1. The avatar is a live WebGL render loop with blink, gaze and a
   mixer running, so two captures of unchanged code differ. There is no exact
   baseline to diff against; the shots are verified by CONTENT (the strings,
   states and geometry each scene claims) rather than by bytes.

scenes.title: A year of conversations.
scenes.caption: You have never once looked at it.
scenes.narration: You have been talking to this thing for a year. You have never once looked at it, because there has never been anything to look at.
scenes._editNote:
The pain, stated as the user actually experiences it. Typographic rather than a screen: the subject of this beat is an ABSENCE, and the only way to shoot an absence is to caption a blank — which is what this card is.

The three em-dashes are the beat, and they set up the title card two scenes later ('A face and a body, in a browser tab.') by naming what is missing first.

They are also load-bearing for the frozen-picture gate. A `feature` with a title and NO items paints once and then holds: both the paced reveal and the drift target the chips row (`.<id>-chips`), so an itemless card has literally nothing in motion for its whole length. Measured on the Companion Scan film in this same rewrite: three itemless cards took that cut to 11% landscape / 14% portrait against an 8% bar, and adding items took it to 0%/0%. Do not strip these back out.

scenes.title: Most people quit right about here.
scenes.caption: The usual price of a face.
scenes.narration: Giving an assistant a face usually means a game engine, a character rig, and a bill that runs by the minute. Most people quit right about here.

scenes._editNote: The title card claims exactly what the following frames carry: a face and a body. The voice claim was moved to the recap, beside the fact that now supports it — see the top-level _honestyNote. A title card is the worst place in a film to put the one claim the pictures cannot back.

shots._focusNote: Focused on the CONNECTION block, which is the beat. It also frames out a real defect at 9:16: mlc has one field fewer than ollama, so the dialog's scroll container lands its boundary mid-row and slices 'WebGPU rendering' through the middle of the glyphs. The committed ollama shot happens to cut cleanly at a divider instead. This is the app's own scroll clipping at 360x640, not a capture artefact, and it is not worth masking — but there is no reason to put it on screen.
shots._captureNote: Establishes onboarding ITSELF (the eval below), for the reason written up on datacenter-diorama: shot order is not a declared dependency and `--only` does not replay it. Selecting `mlc` is the point of the frame, not decoration — FIELD_MAP in SettingsPanel.tsx gives mlc a modelKey and NO urlKey, so the Server URL row disappears and the dialog is visibly a different shape from the Ollama one in `connection`. Nothing is typed here: the model shown is the app's own default (llmConfig.ts defaultLLMConfig.mlc_model), which is the honest thing to film.

scenes.caption: One room ships with it: a 1970s research datacenter.
scenes.narration: Put a room around it, and the camera steps back far enough to bring the whole body into frame.
scenes._editNote: The only environment in the product besides the plain studio — EnvironmentPreset is 'none' | 'datacenter-1970s'. Worded as one room for that reason. The two props whose GLBs do not match their filenames are excluded by PROP_NEEDS_REEXPORT and are not in these frames.

shots.alt: The avatar standing full-length in the 1970s research datacenter: a plotter on a desk, a minicomputer with a printer, a tape reel and cabinets behind
shots._captureNote: Dismisses onboarding ITSELF rather than inheriting it. Every shot after hud-shell used to rely on hud-shell's Skip click having persisted ci_avatar_onboarded into the shared browser context — an ordering dependency nothing declares. It holds for a full run and breaks the moment anyone re-shoots one shot: `make.sh --only datacenter-diorama` captured this frame with the Enable Microphone modal and its blur backdrop over the whole room. The step below is an eval, not a click, because it has to be a no-op on the full run too: by the time this shot runs in order the key is already set, the Skip button does not exist, and a plain click step would fail the run.
shots._poseNote: The wait is 9000, not 3000, and it is about the avatar's ARMS. On load the rig greets (a Waving clip) before it settles into its idle, and the greet is still unwinding at +6s — arms out, fingers spread, which photographs as a mannequin rather than a character. Sampled on Metal at networkidle + N ms: 1000 bind pose, 2500 arms overhead mid-wave, 4000-6000 arms coming down, 10000+ a settled idle with the arms hanging naturally. 9000 + settle 3000 lands well clear of it. See capture.config.mjs hazard 12 for the other half of this — under a software rasteriser the mixer never drives the rig at all and NO settle helps, which is what put the A-pose in the shots this replaced.

shots.alt: The same room with the dock and chat panel collapsed, leaving the avatar full-length in the diorama
shots._focusNote:
push-in, not drift-down, and with a subject. The room only occupies the lower two thirds of the plate — above the machines is unlit ceiling, and it is a third of the 9:16 crop. A drift-down would spend the shot travelling INTO that emptiness. The focus rects instead end the push on the desk-and-avatar band at 16:9 and on the avatar at 9:16, so the move settles on something and the dead air at the top is cropped out rather than approached.

Landscape widened 0.72 -> 0.80 (1.79x -> 1.61x) on 2026-08-07, because the caption of this very scene is "Body included." and the old rectangle cut the avatar at the knee — the shot argued against its own caption. It also slid: at 0.72 the kit reported the window sliding back to y 0.279 from the requested 0.30, and left a fragment of the collapsed Controls button showing under the caption band. At 0.80 the figure reads full-length from head to shin, the far-right machine pair comes back into frame, and nothing slides. The feet are still behind the caption band and cannot be rescued — they sit at y~0.97 of the plate, so no window that keeps the avatar this size clears them. "Body included" is a claim about a full-length framing against the busts everywhere else in the film, which this now supports; it is not a claim about toes.
shots._captureNote: The film's only wide shot, and the only frame in which the avatar has legs. That is not a camera trick in the edit — Scene3D's ENVIRONMENT_LOOK parks the camera at 2.4 m landscape / 3.6 m portrait for `datacenter-1970s`, against 0.5 m for the studio, so every other shot is a bust and no `before` step can widen them (capture.config.mjs hazard 9). Collapsing both panels is what makes it work at 9:16: with the Chat Log rail up, the portrait crop of this room keeps the bust and loses the desk entirely. Establishes onboarding itself — same reason as datacenter-diorama.

scenes.caption: No account. No monthly fee. The cloud is opt-in.
scenes.narration: Five ways to connect a model, a clip library of forty-seven, and speech that falls back to the browser's own. None of it needs an account.
scenes._editNote: 'a clip library of forty-seven' — LIBRARY, deliberately. No single avatar loads all 47 (VRM rigs get 6, GLB rigs 34, feminine rigs the combined set), so any phrasing that attaches the number to the avatar on screen would be false. The speech line is what the ttsService fallback in this PR makes true; before it, a default install was mute.

scenes.narration: Spatial Companion, from Companion Intelligence. UnCloud your life.
